challenges.title: Recall checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Without reopening the lesson, explain Accessibility, Attention, and Pacing Guide in your own words. Include the problem it solves, the core mechanism, and one boundary or failure.
challenges.hint: Use “Keep the target stable and vary the route” as a cue, then close the lesson again.

challenges.title: Prediction checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Choose one example or source file from this mission. Predict its behavior for a normal input and a changed or invalid input before running or revealing the reference. Explain the rule separating the outcomes.
challenges.hint: Change one condition at a time so the result teaches a rule.

challenges.title: Build and prove checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Implement, debug, or adapt the mission exercise yourself. Record the acceptance criterion, command or interaction used to verify it, failure evidence, and one tradeoff. Do not paste the reference solution.
challenges.hint: A passing check, measured result, focused diff, or reproducible demo is stronger than ‘done.’

files.content:
# Accessibility, Attention, and Pacing Guide

This guide reduces avoidable barriers without weakening engineering outcomes.
Use the supports that improve access today; do not interpret them as a diagnosis
or permanent learner category.

## Keep the target stable and vary the route

The stable target is observable capability: retrieve, implement, debug, explain,
and transfer. The route may vary through text, diagrams, examples, narration,
hands-on practice, quiet reflection, collaboration, or smaller time boxes.

## When starting feels too large

Reduce the number of simultaneous decisions:

1. choose one acceptance criterion;
2. choose one input and expected output;
3. choose one file or boundary;
4. write one prediction;
5. run one check;
6. record one next action.

Use a “parking lot” for unrelated ideas. Do not switch tasks to resolve them
during the current time box.

## When reading is a barrier

- Read one heading and its first exercise before the entire explanation.
- Convert paragraphs into a three-column table: claim, example, evidence.
- Use text-to-speech if helpful, then pause to predict before continuing.
- Keep code and explanation side by side, but close both for retrieval.
- Define unfamiliar terms in plain language and one precise technical sentence.
- Use descriptive link text and headings rather than relying on document position.

Reading support must end in a generated response: a prediction, test, changed
example, diagram, or explanation from memory.

## When diagrams help—or do not

- Use shape, label, and line style in addition to color.
- Place a numbered text sequence below every important diagram.
- Keep one question per diagram; split overloaded maps.
- Use state tables when spatial layouts are distracting.
- Test the map by removing a node or changing a failure path.

## When listening or speaking helps

- Record a two-minute explanation and replay it for unsupported claims.
- Narrate code at the level of intent and state change, not punctuation.
- Use five keywords instead of a memorized script.
- Keep a transcript or short written summary for later retrieval.
- Pause recordings before the answer and make a prediction aloud.

Listening alone is exposure. Retrieval, prediction, and changed examples make it
practice.

## When movement and direct manipulation help

- Use cards or sticky notes for queue entries, state transitions, or database
  rows, then simulate retries and concurrency.
- Step through a request physically or with a debugger, naming each boundary.
- Reorder test cases or records and predict what must remain invariant.
- Build the smallest running slice before reading the full deep dive.

Manipulation should reveal a rule that can later be stated and implemented
without the physical aid.

## When live collaboration is demanding

- Share acceptance criteria before the session.
- Allow two quiet minutes to write a prediction before discussion.
- Rotate driver, navigator, and reviewer roles on a visible timer.
- Permit written comments before verbal review.
- End with individual reconstruction so processing speed is not confused with
  understanding.

## When attention or energy varies

### Low-energy work

- no-notes recall of one concept;
- review a small diff;
- improve one test name or assertion;
- fill one trace-table row;
- write one counterexample;
- record one short teach-back;
- schedule spaced review.

### Medium-energy work

- implement one acceptance criterion;
- debug one reproducible failure;
- write an ADR comparison;
- perform an accessibility or authorization pass;
- add an integration test.

### High-energy work

- integrate multiple layers;
- investigate unfamiliar nondeterminism;
- design schema or compatibility changes;
- run load, recovery, or deployment exercises;
- conduct a full system-design review.

Save high-cognitive-load work for suitable sessions rather than interpreting a
bad time slot as inability.

## Interruption recovery card

Before stopping unexpectedly, record:

- current goal;
- last observed evidence;
- current hypothesis;
- exact next command or action;
- unsafe or misleading shortcuts to avoid.

On return, retrieve the goal before reading the card. Then use it to restore
context and confirm whether your remembered model was accurate.

## Pacing options

| Weekly availability | Suggested calendar | Session pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 3–4 hours | 24–30 weeks | four short sessions plus one integration session every two weeks |
| 5–7 hours | 16–20 weeks | three focused sessions and one weekly integration/review |
| 8–12 hours | 12 weeks | standard curriculum rhythm |
| 13+ hours | still at least 12 weeks | add variations, reviews, and deeper capstone scope rather than cramming |

Spacing is part of the training. Completing twelve weeks of material in one
week removes much of the delayed retrieval and recovery practice.

## Environment checklist

- readable font size and comfortable contrast;
- keyboard access and visible focus in tools and the product being built;
- notifications silenced for the time box;
- one visible goal and a defined stop condition;
- commands saved in project documentation, not personal memory;
- captions or transcripts for recorded material;
- breaks planned before accuracy degrades;
- sensitive personal information excluded from shared learning logs.

## Requesting useful support

Ask for a specific change tied to performance:

- “Give me the acceptance criteria before the discussion.”
- “Let me write my prediction before you show the output.”
- “Please provide the diagram as a numbered text sequence too.”
- “Ask one diagnostic question before giving the next hint.”
- “Can we split this review into correctness and maintainability passes?”
- “I need a 10-minute break, then I will reconstruct the current hypothesis.”

## Weekly barrier review

Record one answer for each:

- What barrier consumed effort without improving the engineering skill?
- Which support improved accuracy or independence?
- Which support became passive avoidance?
- What should stay, change, or be removed next week?
- Did the same mastery standard remain intact?
